name: Bianca Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers stay confidential. What fills a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run new electricity connections on the south side of town, where fresh houses meet old buried cable. I fit the cut-out, the main fuse where the supply enters, then test before anyone puts furniture in. Seeing the first kitchen light come on still pleases me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Builders who cover a trench before we have checked it. I learned through a vocational certificate and apprenticeship, so I trust a drawing only after seeing the ground. I sometimes use an AI writing tool to tidy a note, but I recheck every number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the connection crew that the software can tidy our job sheets but it cannot terminate a cable at a new house. A family still wants the lights on when they move in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company has plenty of connections and I have a decent wage. My husband David has his plumbing work, and we have savings beyond six months, though the roof on our flat will need money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would carry on with the south-side connections and use the AI writing tool now and then to clean up my inspection notes. I would put a little extra from each wage into the roof account instead of ordering a new dining table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. I know the trade well enough to spot a wrong note, and there is no rush to change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before using a cleaned-up note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cable size, address and isolation reading. A sentence can sound lovely and still put the wrong house on a safety record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much goes to the roof account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small amount from every pay packet, on top of what we already save. David and I will decide the exact amount after we get a roof quote.

say: The software can tidy **job sheets**, while a lineworker still connects each house safely.
I would tell new families their **lights** still need a human crew on moving day.
think: Our **two incomes** and savings make this world comfortable, even with a roof repair coming.
I would use AI for wording but still check every **safety detail** myself.
do: Keep making **south-side connections** and check the cable details on every job sheet.
Add extra money from each **wage** to the roof account after David and I get a quote.
feel: **Calm**, because the work and household income look stable.
S0.quote: A sentence can sound lovely and still put the wrong house on a safety record.
fieldNote: She accepts a limited **writing aid** while retaining responsibility for electrical checks.
The roof is a real expense, but her **two incomes** and substantial savings leave room to plan.

steps.text: Keep south-side connection shifts and check each safety record
Add extra wages to the roof account after getting a repair quote

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that planners may have fewer calls to make, but builders will still dig in the wrong place. I would ask for a trial before the new AI scheduling screen sends us across town twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could see the office cutting planners first and giving each field crew more connections. My field work feels secure for now, but David’s plumbing enquiries might dip if his customers lose work. My lineworker wage might hold, but I cannot call my husband David’s plumbing income safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test the new AI scheduling screen with a colleague for two weeks and write down journeys it gets wrong. I would also ask David to review the last three months of plumbing bookings before we commit to the dining table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the depot and anxious for our household if David loses bookings. The savings help, but a long thin spell for his business would still change our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a problem with the schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it sends us to a street before the trench is ready, the whole crew loses half a day. I would note the address and time, then show the supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the table if his bookings hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after the roof quote is covered. I would not scrap every purchase over a possibility, but I would wait for actual figures.

say: I would ask for a **scheduling trial** before a screen sends connection crews to unfinished trenches.
I would remind the crew that **builders and cables** still need coordination on site.
think: My field job seems sound, but **David’s plumbing income** could fall if his customers lose work.
Our **savings** cushion a bad spell without making both household incomes certain.
do: Test the **schedule screen** with a colleague for two weeks and record wasted journeys.
Delay the **dining table** until David checks three months of bookings and the roof quote is covered.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost plumbing bookings in the household, despite security in her own field work.
S1.quote: My lineworker wage might hold, but I cannot call my husband David’s plumbing income safe.
fieldNote: She treats the tool as something to **test at work**, not as a reason to abandon the trade.
Her concern is specifically **David’s customer pipeline**, and she waits for bookings before changing a purchase.

steps.text: Test the AI scheduling screen with a colleague for two weeks
Delay the dining table until plumbing bookings and roof costs are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that thinking AI in 2028 does not make a safe connection at a building site. A robot might do that by 2031, and we should see it work on awkward old houses before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office change could be immediate, and I might still have three years of field work. By 2031 I would be sixty three, near the end I planned, but David might face cheaper automated estimates and fewer plumbing jobs sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask David to list his current bookings and cash reserves this month. If his paid work drops for two quarters, we would cut the dining table and the winter trip; I would keep my lineworker hours while they are offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not lost. The house and savings buy time, but a fast fall in his invoices would make me count every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring your retirement date forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on the card alone. I would keep working while the company offers field hours and my body is willing; David and I can review retirement when we know his income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust a connection robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show me an old house with a surprise buried cable, a wet trench and a qualified person checking every isolation point. A showroom house is too easy a test for a connection robot.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** leaves on-site cable work, but a 2031 robot needs a hard field trial.
I would demand tests on **old houses** with messy trenches before using robots near live supply.
think: I may still have field hours until **2031**, while David’s plumbing invoices could weaken sooner.
Our **savings** help, but two weak quarters for his business would force spending choices.
do: Review **David’s bookings** and business cash with him this month.
Cut the **table and trip** if his paid plumbing work falls for two quarters.
Keep **connection shifts** while the company offers them and my body allows.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough savings to plan through a fast household income change.
S2.quote: A showroom house is too easy a test for a connection robot.
fieldNote: She locates the immediate risk in **David’s invoices**, while her own hands-on job has a three-year robot lag.
She gives a **two-quarter threshold** for spending cuts and does not claim she will retire early.

steps.text: Cut the dining table and winter trip after two weak plumbing quarters
Keep connection shifts while offered and physically manageable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to test robot connections in bad conditions, if the company starts with real streets. I would want the crew to see the test results, not just a sales film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am likely to be out of regular line work before 2034 on our current plan. David’s plumbing business may still be working, though, and the thinking AI in 2031 could change how people book and price his jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep connecting houses next year and show the younger crew how I check a cut-out, the main fuse at the supply entrance. David and I would review his prices and bookings every six months, then change our spending only if the figures turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own wage for now, uneasy about his business later. Five years lets us watch actual demand instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new business system for David now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. He already uses a simple booking calendar, and I would want evidence that a paid system earns its cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you pass to younger lineworkers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to stop when the plans and the trench disagree. I can show a new colleague the cut-out once; then I make them point out every connection themselves.

say: I would want **real-street trials** and results shared with the crew before robot connections begin in 2034.
I would teach younger workers the **supply checks** a sales film cannot demonstrate.
think: My **regular line work** may finish before the robots arrive under our current plan.
David’s **plumbing bookings** could change when thinking AI affects customers and pricing in 2031.
do: Keep **connecting houses** next year and teach younger workers to check the main fuse.
Review **plumbing prices and bookings** with David every six months before changing household spending.
feel: **Calm** about her own wage now, with unease about David’s business later.
S3.quote: I would want the crew to see the test results, not just a sales film.
fieldNote: Her planned work exit precedes the **robot date** without being brought forward by it.
She favours a **six-month review** of David’s actual trade over an immediate purchase or retraining course.

steps.text: Keep connecting houses and teach new crew members main fuse checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew the ten years are a gift if we use them to train careful people. The machines in 2039 can wait for proper site tests; nobody should waive an electrical check because a robot looks neat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be retired on our present timetable before 2036 if the roof and our savings stay in shape. David’s work might run longer, and I cannot tell what plumbing customers will want ten years from now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the next year, starting now in 2026, I would stay on the south-side connections and put the new starter beside me on old-house jobs. I would also get the roof quote with David, so our planned retirement rests on a real cost. After thinking AI arrives in 2036, I would follow our retirement plan if the figures hold; if I am still employed, I would keep those physical checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There is time to settle our own accounts and leave the trade with a careful pair of hands behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 2036 date change when you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our date depends on the house, our savings and our health, not the AI calendar. If the roof costs more than expected, I may work longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the new starter at the last old-house job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the new starter that a neat drawing is only the start. Open the electrical supply box, test the power and make your own record before trusting an AI drawing.

say: Ten years lets us train **careful lineworkers** before thinking AI and later robots reshape the job.
I would require **site tests** before a 2039 robot could sign off electrical connections.
think: Our **retirement plan** likely ends my field work before 2036 if the roof and savings permit.
David’s **plumbing work** may last longer, and future customer demand remains uncertain.
do: **Keep** south-side connection shifts now, teaching physical checks, and continue only if still employed after 2036.
Get a **roof quote** with David to check our existing retirement figures.
feel: **Calm**, with enough time to settle household costs and pass on careful work habits.
S4.quote: Open the electrical supply box, test the power and make your own record before trusting an AI drawing.
fieldNote: Her retirement timing remains tied to the **roof cost** and existing plan, not the card date.
She uses the long runway to **teach on site**, consistent with her practical openness to proven tools.

steps.text: Keep connection work and teach physical checks now and after 2036 if still employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because David, my husband, might lose plumbing bookings while my own field work is still there. Seeing the company test robots on awkward houses and having a clear view of his invoices would help us make sensible choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the younger person standing beside me. I can probably finish my career, but practical teaching matters. A new starter needs more than a nice video of a robot making one easy connection.

headlineQuote: A new starter needs more than a nice video of a robot making one easy connection.
portrait: **Bianca**, 58, is a mid-level connection lineworker with apprenticeship training, higher pay and a practical interest in proven tools.
She and her husband have **two incomes** and more than six months saved, though a roof repair will draw on their funds.
She occasionally uses **AI writing help** but checks safety readings herself and wants field evidence before adopting scheduling or robots.
Her **2028 worry** centres on David’s plumbing bookings, while she expects her hands-on electrical work to last longer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her husband’s plumbing bookings before robots reach her own connection work.
whatWouldHelp: A clear view of **plumbing invoices** and field trials on awkward houses would help them plan.
